```{r m6-setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", out.width = "100%")
options(width = 82)
fmt <- function(x, digits = 3) formatC(x, digits = digits, format = "f")
```

Posterior uncertainty, numerical approximation error and model adequacy
refer to different aspects of an analysis. An accurately computed posterior
may leave the ordering of two entities uncertain. Similarly, optimization
can be accurate for coefficients that are themselves estimated imprecisely.
We distinguish these sources of uncertainty when interpreting the
available diagnostics.

The calculations use two small bundled inputs: IID draws from a specified
normal law and MCMC output with recorded chain history from a known
two-state law. Both are simulation examples rather than empirical studies,
and neither model fitting nor optimization is performed here.

## Pairwise Monte Carlo standard errors {#start-with-one-direction-on-one-criterion}

For the claim that entity i has higher priority than j on criterion k,
the directional-error probability is the posterior mean of
`theta[i,k] <= theta[j,k]`. A probability near one half describes uncertainty
about that direction under the supplied law. A Monte Carlo standard error
(MCSE) describes uncertainty in estimating the probability from a finite
simulation. Increasing the simulation size can reduce MCSE without making
the posterior direction any more certain.

The object `postrank_toy` contains 32 IID whole-state draws for three
fictional sites and two criteria. The following calculation selects the
`need_A` comparison from `001` to `site-B`; the diagnostic therefore applies
to this specified pair rather than to every pair.

```{r m6-iid-pair}
library(postrank)
pair <- data.frame(entity_i = "001", entity_j = "site-B",
  criterion_id = "need_A")
iid_diagnostic <- postrank_diagnose(postrank_toy, pairs = pair)
pair_summary <- iid_diagnostic$summaries$pair_1
z_iid <- iid_diagnostic$traces$pair_1$values
iid_table <- data.frame(
  Draws = length(z_iid), Estimated_probability = mean(z_iid),
  MCSE = pair_summary$diagnostics$mcse_mean$value,
  Direct_SD_over_sqrt_S = sd(z_iid) / sqrt(length(z_iid)))
knitr::kable(iid_table, digits = 4)
```

For IID output, the MCSE is the sample standard deviation divided by
the square root of the number of retained states. For a binary trace this
is `sqrt(p_hat * (1 - p_hat) / (S - 1))`. It estimates pointwise numerical
precision and supplies neither a simultaneous interval over pairs nor a
probability that the grade report is correct. The small draw count is used
for illustration and is not a recommended simulation size.

A posterior interval describes the target distribution under the model,
whereas an interval for Monte Carlo error concerns the numerical estimate
of a functional of that distribution. The distinction is developed in
[Chapter 15, “Monte Carlo error under a declared sampling law”](https://joonho112.github.io/postrank-theory-book/chapters/15-numerical-uncertainty.html#sec-monte-carlo-coefficients).

## Loss traces for a fixed report {#diagnose-the-loss-of-a-declared-report}

For a fixed grade vector, `postrank_diagnose()` also forms criterion error
and risk traces. With joint draws, it combines criterion losses **within
each same posterior state** to obtain a weighted total-loss trace. This
preserves their covariance, which generally precludes combining separate
criterion MCSEs under an independence assumption.

The next example uses `pr_toy_mcmc`, four independent chains of 512
iterations each, initialized from their stationary law. Its producer uses
transition probabilities .012 from state 0 to state 1 and .048 in reverse.
Thus the stationary state-1 probability is .2, but successive states are
strongly correlated. The data are stored chain by chain, with no warmup
or thinning. These sampling properties are specified by the generator and cannot be
inferred from an array without its chain records.

```{r m6-mcmc}
law <- attr(pr_toy_mcmc, "law")
mcmc <- postrank_draws(pr_toy_mcmc, regime = "mcmc", chains = 4L,
  warmup_per_chain = 0L, thin = 1L, declarations = law$declarations)
grade <- c(A = 1L, B = 2L, C = 3L)
settings <- list(weights = c(k1 = .6, k2 = .4), tau = .25)
diagnostic <- postrank_diagnose(mcmc, grade = grade, settings = settings,
  pairs = data.frame(entity_i = "A", entity_j = "B", criterion_id = "k1"))
selected_summaries <- diagnostic$summaries[c("pair_1", "weighted_total_loss")]
diagnostic_table <- do.call(rbind, lapply(selected_summaries, function(s)
  data.frame(Mean = s$mean, MCSE = s$diagnostics$mcse_mean$value,
    ESS_mean = s$diagnostics$ess_mean$value,
    Rhat = s$diagnostics$rhat$value,
    ESS_tail = s$diagnostics$ess_tail$value)))
rownames(diagnostic_table) <- c("A above B: k1 error", "Fixed report: weighted loss")
knitr::kable(diagnostic_table, digits = 4)
```

The pair trace is exactly the state-1 indicator: its pooled mean is
353/2048 = `r fmt(diagnostic_table$Mean[1], 4)`, versus .2 under the known
law. The fixed report's loss is `2/15 + (2/3) * indicator`, so its exact
expected loss is 4/15. Its estimated loss is
`r fmt(diagnostic_table$Mean[2], 4)`. The MCSE scales by 2/3 as well. This
simple identity checks the diagnostic against the underlying states;
it does not claim that this report is optimal.

Criterion traces remain available separately as
`diagnostic$summaries$criterion_risk_1` and `criterion_risk_2`. With
criterionwise inputs, criterion diagnostics can be available while a
joint total-loss MCSE is unavailable: separate blocks do not establish
their simulation covariance. For minimax, the returned weighted total
trace is auxiliary; it is not an implemented MCSE for the maximum of
expected criterion risks.

## Interpretation of MCMC diagnostics {#what-the-mcmc-metrics-actually-summarize}

For eligible equal-length chains the package calls `posterior::rhat`,
`ess_bulk`, `ess_tail`, `ess_mean`, and `mcse_mean`. The installed
`posterior` methods use split chains: R-hat combines rank-normalized and
folded checks, bulk ESS concerns the rank-normalized distribution, and
tail ESS uses the smaller of the .05 and .95 quantile ESS values.
Mean ESS describes precision of the mean; `mcse_mean` uses the trace's
sample SD divided by its square root. These scalar diagnostics are not
the multivariate determinant ESS described in
[Chapter 15, “Multivariate output analysis and effective sample size”](https://joonho112.github.io/postrank-theory-book/chapters/15-numerical-uncertainty.html#sec-mcmc-output-analysis).

For this binary trace, tail diagnostics encounter degenerate quantile
indicators. The table retains the resulting `NA`. Metric records include
`available`, `unavailable_reason`, `result_kind`, warnings and the method;
unavailable is not zero. Similarly, an observed constant trace can mean
that a rare state has never been visited. Zero empirical variation is not
proof of zero posterior probability or adequate exploration.

The supplied history preserves original chain IDs and retained iteration
numbers. Unequal chains keep every value in their pooled means, but the
package does not calculate cross-chain MCSE, ESS or R-hat by truncating
or padding them. One chain cannot establish independent-chain agreement.
The package's R-hat 1.01 and ESS 100-per-chain guidelines flag potential
limitations in exploration; they do not establish convergence or
finite-sample coverage.

In this run, R-hat is `r fmt(diagnostic_table$Rhat[1], 4)`, above 1.01.
Mean and bulk ESS are both `r fmt(diagnostic_table$ESS_mean[1], 2)`, below
the guideline of 400 across four chains. The three stored warnings concern chain exploration and mean precision
and are available in `diagnostic$warnings`.

```{r m6-chain-comparison}
pair_trace <- diagnostic$traces$pair_1$values
chain_means <- diagnostic$summaries$pair_1$chain_means
knitr::kable(data.frame(Chain = names(chain_means),
  Estimated_probability = unname(chain_means)), digits = 4, row.names = FALSE)
c(MCMC_MCSE = diagnostic_table$MCSE[1],
  Incorrect_IID_reference = sd(pair_trace) / sqrt(length(pair_trace)))
```

The IID reference is substantially smaller because it ignores serial
dependence. Substituting an estimated ESS for S in an IID concentration
inequality is not justified. The dependent-chain theorem in the book
instead requires stationarity, reversibility and a justified full-chain
spectral-gap bound. Neither an empirical ESS nor a chosen burn-in supplies
these constants, and the implementation does not provide a general finite-sample
certificate for MCMC output.

## Fixed and selected actions {#a-fixed-action-and-a-selected-action-need-different-interpretations}

The grade above was supplied explicitly. When a `fit` is supplied instead,
the diagnostic verifies its input and grade identities, uses its settings,
and marks the summaries as descriptive after selection from the same draws.
Pointwise MCSE for that realized grade does not automatically give coverage
after searching for the best grade. Even an explicit `grade` declaration
does not let the software verify how the analyst selected it.

If every comparison is withheld, ordinary weighted loss is the constant
`tau` at every state. There is then no loss variation to diagnose, although
the latent targets may remain uncertain and chains may mix poorly. The
object records `structural_constant_from_action`; conditional error ratios
remain `NA` because N=0. Constant-action loss is different from an observed
constant pair indicator.

Probability-only inputs and supplied marginal means or intervals contain
no recoverable simulation history. Chain records and MCSE therefore cannot be recovered from these inputs.
Typed mixture diagnostics, when supported with genuine hyperstate history,
describe integration of **conditional expected risk**, not latent
target-loss dispersion. Fixed Gaussian or finite-mixture representations
do not by themselves imply a Monte Carlo sample count. See
[Posterior inputs](m3-posterior-inputs.html) for those distinctions.

## Sensitivity analysis and cross-fitting {#sensitivity-and-cross-fitting-answer-narrower-questions}

`postrank_mc_fragility()` compares the estimated weighted loss from disclosure
in a pair's better direction with the withholding cost. The absolute difference
from `tau` is compared with a multiple of the MCSE of that direction's weighted
indicator.
The grade report is chosen jointly, so a fragile pair need not change a
grade. Screening and multiplier choices are reported. The default MCMC
screen margin .1 is a computational screening rule and does not bound
the omitted pairs.

Stability requests in `postrank_diagnose()` run additional optimizations
on declared prefixes, chain subsets or settings. Overlapping subsets are
not independent replications. Changed grades can reflect numerical noise,
policy changes, multiple optima or optimization gaps; unchanged grades
do not prove convergence. The record keeps failed and no-incumbent
attempts alongside successful ones. These solves are optional and are not
run in this article.

`postrank_crossfit()` instead selects a grade on each of two folds and
evaluates it on the other. IID inputs use stored halves; MCMC uses groups
of whole chains, or halves when only one chain exists. With independent
target-IID folds and loss settings fixed independently of evaluation
draws, out-of-fold **linear weighted risk** is conditionally unbiased for
the training fold's selected grade. Its difference from in-fold risk
concerns that fold grade, not the optimism of the full-data grade.

The argument does not extend to the nonlinear maximum used by minimax.
For MCMC, splitting whole chains alone establishes neither independence
nor stationarity. Cross-fitting reuses the supplied fitted model; it is
not refitting on held-out observations or testing external calibration.
If both folds choose the same grade, signed differences cancel, so zero
mean optimism need not mean precision; `mean_abs_optimism` retains scale.
The fold statuses identify how many evaluations contributed to the
summary; a result from one available fold supplies only one evaluation.
Neither summary corrects the full-data risk.

## Conditional IID coefficient bounds {#conditional-iid-bounds-cover-a-different-calculation}

For fixed-size IID sampling, a simultaneous coefficient envelope can
cover an action selected using those same coefficients. The package's
tie-free setting makes reverse directions complementary. With
`M = choose(n, 2)` and positive prespecified allocations summing to at
most alpha, its criterion radius is

\[
\varepsilon_k = \min\left\{1,
 \sqrt{\frac{\log(2M/\alpha_k)}{2S_k}}\right\}.
\]

The broader equality-permitting theorem in the book counts both ordered
directions and uses `4M`, not `2M`. Its scope must not be inferred from
the runtime's smaller factor. The separate equality-neutral mode does
not currently supply these diagnostic or bound helpers.

The bundled normal generator prespecified S=32 and the following error
allocations before sampling. These design declarations are therefore
available for this example:

```{r m6-iid-bound}
bounds <- postrank_iid_bounds(postrank_toy, alpha = .05,
  alpha_by_criterion = c(need_A = .025, need_B = .025),
  design = list(sample_sizes_fixed_before_sampling = TRUE,
    alpha_fixed_before_sampling = TRUE, adaptive_stopping = FALSE,
    planned_sample_sizes = c(need_A = 32L, need_B = 32L),
    declaration_note = "Prespecified in the bundled synthetic Normal generator"))
knitr::kable(data.frame(Criterion = names(bounds$epsilon),
  Radius = unname(bounds$epsilon)), digits = 4)
bounds[c("guarantee_status", "guarantee_issued", "numerically_verified")]
```

The probability statement is over repeated fixed-size Monte Carlo runs
conditional on the supplied law and observed information. It is not a
posterior probability that a grade is right. Draws must be independent
across whole states within each criterion; pairs and criteria need not
be independent of one another. Sampling sizes and error allocations must
be fixed in advance, with no adaptive stopping. A declaration records
these assumptions; it does not verify them. The result is a floating
reference `conditional_bound`; formal guarantee and numerical-verification
flags remain false.

On such a coefficient event, write `delta_w = sum(w * epsilon)`. Risk error
for a fixed action is at most `(N/M) * delta_w`. For the **same fixed action
family**, an empirical optimizer with a valid whole-problem absolute
risk gap eta has supplied-law regret at most `2 * delta_w + eta`.
`postrank_regret_bound()` checks eligible weighted fits, matching inputs
and usable gap information; it does not turn a candidate-only, raw or
relative gap into that eta. The bound concerns risk, not agreement of
grade vectors. It excludes empirically protected problems from this
common-family calculation.

Protection needs a separate construction: inner rows use
`E_hat_k <= (q_k - epsilon_k) * N`, outer rows use the plus sign.
The signed thresholds are not clipped to zero. A negative inner threshold
can exclude all positive disclosure without proving the intended protected
problem infeasible. Zero-weight protected criteria still need their own
radii. Protection analysis combines a validated inner action with a lower
bound for the **whole outer problem**, not the inner lower bound or outer
incumbent. These additional optimizations are not run in this article. The helpers retain
diagnostic rather than formal certification flags. Full derivations and
the current implementation distinction appear in
[Chapter 15](https://joonho112.github.io/postrank-theory-book/chapters/15-numerical-uncertainty.html#sec-coefficient-error)
and [Appendix D](https://joonho112.github.io/postrank-theory-book/appendices/D-package-correspondence.html#conditional-numerical-helpers).

## Numerical accuracy and model adequacy {#numerical-accuracy-leaves-model-adequacy-to-be-assessed}

Solver gaps provide numerical bounds on suboptimality for the declared
problem. MCSEs and coefficient envelopes quantify aspects of its
approximation to the supplied law. These measures do not assess the
difference between that law and an external population: greater numerical
precision can coexist with model misspecification. The distinction is
examined in
[Chapter 18, “Self-reported error and calibration”](https://joonho112.github.io/postrank-theory-book/chapters/18-misspecification-calibration.html#sec-self-reported-calibration).

In plug-in empirical Bayes, posterior calculations condition on the fitted
mixing distribution, often written `G_hat`. This is not the grade cap G.
More posterior draws with `G_hat` fixed do not include uncertainty from
estimating it. Hierarchical integration propagates the uncertainty specified
by that model, but does not establish its external calibration. A
repeated-data evaluation of a fitting procedure must repeat estimation,
transformations and data-dependent settings, rather than freeze them
across datasets.

Simulation results concern their stated generating laws and fitting
rules. Independent datasets, not pairs or posterior arms from the same
dataset, supply independent replications. Such results do not furnish a
universal bias correction or make small reported risks calibrated in a
new application. Diagnostics inform numerical work; assessment of targets,
measurement and model adequacy requires the scientific evidence described
in [Chapter 18, “Hyperparameters, precision and represented uncertainty”](https://joonho112.github.io/postrank-theory-book/chapters/18-misspecification-calibration.html#sec-producer-model-error).

[Computing grades](m5-computing-grades.html) describes numerical statuses
and gaps. [True ties and withheld comparisons](m4-ties-and-withholding.html)
distinguishes shared grades from latent equality.
